TideBreaker – A New Frontier in Unmanned Electric Surface Vessels

TideBreaker: A Robotics Club of Central Florida Approach to the
2026 “Promoting Electrical Propulsion” Competition
Dylan Kaney (Project Lead), Caicheng Li, Joshua Fernando, Matthew Barrs, Et al.

Abstract
Building upon the previously developed “Rapid3D” unmanned electric
platform, in this paper we explore current frontiers in fully additively
manufactured maritime design for the Promoting Electrical Propulsion (PEP)
national competition hosted by the American Society of Naval Engineers
(ASNE). Leveraging our prior experience in controlled, semi-autonomous marine
robotics, this work introduces significant advancements in active convective
electronic cooling, full-system modularity, robust composites for coating polymer
hulls, and integrated electrical protection architecture in salt/brackish water
environments for our vessel. These improvements were motivated by prior
limitations, especially in electronic reliability, cooling efficiency and wateringress resistant physical design. The new vessel incorporates a completely
overhauled “midsection,” which integrates a modular air-intake chamber and
manifold with additional hardpoints for equipment. The propulsion system was
overhauled with a new pod motor mount and rudder gearbox. The pontoons of
this vessel (inherently a catamaran) were standardized to shorten the BOM and
modified to provide additional hardpoints for tow and transit, while the
electronics were installed in a new enclosure and rewired to include an additional
fuse and redundant E-stops.

TideBreaker – A New Frontier in Unmanned Electric Surface Vessels

Introduction and Background
Our team has extensive exposure to marine robotics, with many members having been on
the Promoting Electrical Propulsion (PEP) competition team at the Robotics Club of Central
Florida (RCCF) for at least five semesters consecutively. This wealth of experience from senior
members and subsystem leads, along with the dedication of rising members, creates a revolving
mentorship structure that has materially enabled the technical results herein and the efficient
knowledge transfer across subsystem development. Access to in-house 3D-printing capabilities,
advanced telemetry and guidance electronics, and access to dedicated fabrication facilities
further supports our iterative design process, allowing future successive teams to refine the
current platform for the first time since RCCF initially engaged in the competition in 2024. More
directly, our approach this year builds on last year's design “Rapid3D,” incorporating innovative
changes that make “TideBreaker” more capable and more reliable.
Electronic propulsion systems and fully unmanned maritime vehicles have been a focus
of many industries in both the private and public sectors for many decades. Private interest in
this technology correlates with the demand for zero-carbon-impact tourist transport, shipping,
and ferrying [2],[3], with military applications becoming consistently realized for small formfactor Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) in recent years due primarily to armed conflict in
eastern Europe [1] and the Black Sea. Fully electric propulsion is a valid system for large vessels
with advanced power-storage and generation technologies such as nuclear reactors but remains
problematic for small to mid-sized vessels that struggle with towing significant payloads without
sacrificing power delivery and lifespan. Our team addresses some of these challenges with
TideBreaker, our ~7ft electric catamaran.

pages.text:
TideBreaker – A New Frontier in Unmanned Electric Surface Vessels

for gearing and active cooling while reducing internal hull volume requirements. The chosen
APISQUEEN 70167 E-foil motor delivers approximately 10.1 horsepower, providing sufficient
power to meet mission requirements. This outboard, direct-drive configuration differs from
conventional USV systems, which often rely on internally mounted motors and shaft-driven
propulsion.
As a direct-drive system, the propeller is mounted directly to the motor, making its design
critical to overall efficiency. Key parameters include blade pitch and diameter, which govern
thrust generation and hydrodynamic performance [6]. Larger diameters and higher pitch increase
thrust and displaced volume per revolution but also require greater torque, resulting in increased
current draw. Blade geometry further influences efficiency by reducing cavitation and
turbulence. The optimization of these factors represents a key improvement in TideBreaker over
Rapid3D, enabling more efficient propulsion while balancing power consumption and
performance.
Additive Manufacturing & Hull Design
Hull design is perhaps the most impactful factor determining the performance of a marine
vessel. The shape of the hull, specifically the length of its waterline, directly correlates with its
maximum efficient speed [7]. To properly manufacture any hull that is designed, regardless of
how optimized its shape is, it is necessary to design it such that it can be manufactured. The hull,
being one of the most important elements to optimize, requires specific, smooth-flowing
geometry for optimal results.
Rapid3D’s hull was fully manufactured using additive manufacturing, aside from its
composite coating and internal supports. This enabled the realization of complex hull geometries
and rapid iteration during development. This manufacturing approach was retained in
TideBreaker, which incorporates previously developed 3D-printed pontoons alongside newly
designed components, including a redesigned midsection. The implications of this manufacturing
method for design constraints are discussed in later sections. The hull geometry is constrained by
the size of its largest internal components, including four 12.8V LiFePO₄ batteries with widths
exceeding 300mm. Additional constraints include the integration of internal structural supports
and the requirement for a watertight outer skin with sufficient thickness. These factors impose
volumetric limits on the hull and directly influence its overall dimensions and layout.

Design and Analysis
The design of TideBreaker was constrained and heavily influenced by the design of
Rapid3D, which itself was heavily influenced by the P1 Offshore Racing organization. Many
companies design and fabricate racing catamarans to compete at competitions hosted by P1. The
team initially drew inspiration from several of these catamarans, and the first CAD models of
Rapid3D were modeled after them in SolidWorks.

Figure 1 - A racing catamaran for the 222 Offshore Australia team which finished runners-up in
the 2019 Class 1 Championship [9]
Designing the new Hull
Using Rapid3D’s hull design, the team identified key areas of improvement after failures
at the PEP 2025 competition. Most impactful of these failures was a software glitch causing the
rudder control system to fail, but equally dubious was the design of the old midsection. This first
design had incorporated a static or otherwise impossible-to-modify air intake chamber; more
interestingly, the inlet was positioned at the lower bow of the midsection. Since the radiator is
housed in the chamber connecting the inlet to the outlet, airflow through the chamber is
necessary for cooling and thus continued operation.

Figure 2 - A cross-section of Rapid3D's midsection showing the air intake chamber

at the PEP 2025 competition. Most impactful of these failures was a software glitch causing the

pages.text:
TideBreaker – A New Frontier in Unmanned Electric Surface Vessels

Figure 3 - Relative radiator location in Rapid3D midsection shown by green box
The choice to position the inlet at the bottom of the midsection was motivated by the
desire to have the midsection and pontoons ram air into the inlet and from there into the radiator,
which theoretically would improve the efficiency of convective cooling as the boat accelerates
forward. However, given the instability of the waterline height during forward movement on
turbulent water, the inlet is equally likely to cause water ingress when the waterline rises above
it. This flaw is not catastrophic in either design, as the intake chamber is compartmentalized and
isolated from the sensitive electronics housed in the cavity behind it. However, as the radiator is
part of an active cooling loop, water pooling around the cooling lines (which do penetrate the
chamber wall) may cause water to leak into the cavity which houses the electronics. Moreover,
water preventing airflow in the chamber can cause the radiator to overheat in extreme
circumstances and, in other cases, cause a reduction in cooling efficiency which can bottleneck
future low-voltage system modifications that may generate more heat.
Midsection Modifications
Given that the old midsection incorporated a static air intake, a complete redesign and
refabrication was necessary to correct the geometry. The new air intake would be modular,
including a removable intake “lid” and six hardpoints that interface with M6 bolts, allowing
future modifications to be easily attached and removed.

Figure 4 - Isometric view of the new (TideBreaker) midsection with the radiator chamber
exposed
The new midsection, shown in Figure 4, places the intake chamber on the top of the bow
of the midsection. This offers many advantages, the most important of which is that it is much
less vulnerable to airflow obstruction due to a rising waterline. It also improves maintainability
as the radiator chamber is more easily accessible given the removable lid. Three of six screw
holes are also visible, the implementation of which are elaborated on in a later section.
The new midsection also includes geometry at the stern that accommodates the
emergency stop switch and a new water-resistant high-current 3-pin connector, which is also
elaborated on in a future section.
Pontoon Modifications
The pontoons were also modified from their original forms, but a full redesign of each
was not made necessary given the extent of the modifications. There were two primary structural
modifications made to the pontoons of TideBreaker. The first such modification was the
implementation of a tow bridle connecting both pontoons to comply with Rule 13 of the
Uncrewed-Open division rules for 2026, which stipulates that catamarans must have a towing
bridle that connects to both pontoons for support accessibility purposes.

pages.text:
TideBreaker – A New Frontier in Unmanned Electric Surface Vessels

Figure 5 - A tow-line hull anchor point, attached to the port-side pontoon
To implement the towing bridle, a primary towline was first selected to connect both
pontoons to a central carabiner, which interfaces with the external towing line. The selected
towline consists of a polymer-laminated 0.25-inch steel cable, chosen for its strength and
durability. This cable is internally anchored to the horizontal support beams within each pontoon,
ensuring that towing loads are transferred directly to the structural framework rather than the
outer hull or other sensitive components.
To facilitate load transfer at the hull interface, a composite anchor point was designed
and fabricated using additive manufacturing. These anchor points are mounted externally at the
lower bow of each pontoon. Their primary function is to redistribute towing forces, preventing
localized stress concentrations that would otherwise be applied directly to the pontoon skin and
increase the risk of structural failure during dynamic maneuvers. The anchor assembly consists
of a rigid PETG structure combined with a flexible TPU grommet, forming a compliant interface
that both distributes load and mitigates direct contact between the steel cable and the hull. An
85A TPU material was selected to balance flexibility and stiffness, allowing it to elastically
deform under load while resisting shear forces induced by cable tension and rapid directional
changes. PETG was selected for the rigid components due to material availability and established
printer calibration.
The final modification to the towing bridle system was the integration of an internal
vertical tension rod. This component is mounted to the longitudinal structural extrusions within
the pontoons and serves to redirect towing forces away from non-structural components, such as

The second modification made to the pontoons was the implementation of a standardized
“battery lid” structure. The pontoons of Rapid3D each contain two batteries. These batteries are
protected by a lid as shown in Figure 6. These lids are prone to breaking when they fall, so
printing spares for redundancy is necessary. Since the front lids and back lids are geometrically
distinct and non-superimposable in Rapid3D’s design, each lid requires its own specific spare,
which provides a significant BOM challenge. To address this, the team decided to create an
adapter for each of the distinct lids, which loft the distinct curvature of each lid to a standard, flat
rectangular lid, as seen in Figure 7.

Propulsion Redesign
Rapid3D’s outboard propulsion system was mounted on a lateral aluminum extrusion at
the rear of the midsection, perpendicular to the direction of travel. This extrusion also acted to
connect both pontoons; however, the propulsion system could not be adjusted forward nor
backward to change the center of pressure, which is impactful for proper hydrodynamic
performance. TideBreaker’s propulsion system was designed to mount to a longitudinal
aluminum extrusion to mitigate exactly this problem, with the motor positioned forward from the
rudder.

Figure 8 - Position of rudder and longitudinal extrusion on the underside of TideBreaker's
midsection.

Fabrication
Given the selection of commercially available 3D-printers at the time Rapid3D was being
produced; to maximize print volume and printing speed for our many 3D-printing manufacturing
tasks, we chose the Neptune 4 Max by Elegoo. It has a print volume with dimensions 16.5 x 16.5
x 18.9in^3 and a maximum print speed of 500 mm/s, which is a comfortably fast printing pace
given that the average at the time was closer to 150mm/s.
The first and least time-consuming task was to procure and attach the battery adapters
and new lids. The second and most time-consuming task was to print, assemble and install the
new midsection. The battery adapters could be printed in singular pieces and installed
immediately thereafter, while the midsection had to be printed in several sections over several
weeks and assembled before installation.

Figure 9 - The fully assembled midsection

from that used in Rapid3D. The original Rapid3D design emphasized full modularity, allowing
the pontoons and midsection to be interchanged. While this approach improved flexibility, it
introduced structural weaknesses, and the silicone-based adhesive used at the interfaces degraded
over time. To address these issues, the new midsection was permanently bonded to the pontoons.

Rule 19
Rule 19 of the 2026 competition guidelines requires unmanned vessels to maintain
positive buoyancy in the event of a hull breach. To meet this requirement, remaining cavities
within the pontoons and forward midsection were filled with closed-cell polyurethane foam. The
fully loaded vessel is estimated to weigh 250–300 lbs, with pontoon volume exceeding 6 ft³ after
accounting for onboard components. Based on Archimedes’ principle, approximately 5.6 ft³ of
foam is sufficient to support 350 lb, representing a conservative fully flooded condition with
additional external load. The implementation of polyurethane foam in this manner ensures that
our vessel is safely in compliance with rule 19 and can respond in the event of a hull breach.

approximately 0.5 liters per hour, was later observed during shoreline testing and subsequently
repaired. Following the flood test, dry-land testing of the electronic systems was carried out. The
propulsion, rudder, and primary control systems operated as intended; however, the guidance and
telemetry subsystems exhibited software-related issues, including incomplete communication
between the microcontroller, GPS module, and control system. After addressing initial
integration steps, the fully assembled system proceeded to shoreline testing for further
evaluation, where it performed well despite the leak and lapse in software communication.
Challenges & Risks
Challenges Mitigated
The project encountered several technical and logistical risks associated with modifying a
fully additively manufactured vessel, which were addressed through iterative design and testing.
A primary challenge arose during assembly when the initial epoxy bonding of the newly
fabricated midsection to the existing pontoons failed, resulting in leakage and unintended
material accumulation that required extensive post-processing. This highlighted the sensitivity of
adhesive bonding in large-format printed components and led to improved surface preparation
and application methods. Additional risks were identified during fabrication planning, where
outsourcing to GoEngineer for industrial additive manufacturing was initially considered but
ultimately rejected due to cost, lead time, and limited iteration flexibility. The transition to inhouse 3D printing improved control and turnaround time but introduced new challenges,
including printer reliability, dimensional accuracy, and build volume constraints, all of which
required careful management.
Controllable Risks
The rudder gearbox represents a remaining controllable risk factor in vessel performance.
Due to the inherent limitations and variability associated with additively manufactured gears,
some uncertainty remains regarding long-term reliability. Although the gearbox is expected to
perform adequately throughout the competition, there is potential for tooth skipping or gear
slippage, which could result in unintended steering behavior. Additional controllable risks are
primarily associated with the control system and the integrity of the composite coating. In all
cases, appropriate fail-safe mechanisms have been implemented to mitigate the impact of
potential catastrophic failures.
